'''''Alocasia cucullata''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the '''arum''' family, ''[[Araceae]]''.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:84151-1 |title= Alocasia cucullata (Lour.) G.Don |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=July 3, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/C2VC |title= Alocasia cucullata (Lour.) G.Don |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=July 3, 2025}}</ref> It is known by the common names '''Chinese taro''', '''Chinese ape''', '''Buddha's hand''', and '''hooded dwarf elephant ear'''. It is kept as an [[ornamental plant]].

The native range of the species is unclear, as it is known only from cultivation and from specimens growing around human habitation and in disturbed areas.<ref name=pier>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/alocasia_cucullata.htm ''Alocasia cucullata''.] USFS. Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER).</ref><ref name=ntbg>[http://ntbg.org/plants/plant_details.php?plantid=387 ''Alocasia cucullata''.] National Tropical Botanical Garden.</ref><ref name=boyce>Boyce, P. C. (2008). [http://web3.dnp.go.th/botany/PDF/publications/TFB36.pdf A review of ''Alocasia'' (Araceae: Colocasieae) for Thailand including a novel species and new species records from South-West Thailand.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100827011714/http://web3.dnp.go.th/botany/PDF/publications/TFB36.pdf |date=2010-08-27 }} ''Thai Forest Bulletin'' 36 1-17.</ref> It is grown in many parts of Asia, such as [[China]], [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]], and [[Burma]].<ref name=pier/>

==Description==
This aroid plant is a perennial herb producing thick, erect stems up to 6 centimeters wide that branch from the bases and grow up to a meter tall. It produces bunches of leaves on long, sheathed [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] which are generally up to about 30 centimeters long but are known to reach 80. The wide, roughly heart-shaped leaf blade is up to 40 by 28 centimeters and has 4 main veins running from the center to the edge on each side. The plant rarely flowers. When it develops, the [[inflorescence]] may be solitary or paired. It arises on a [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] 20 to 30 centimeters long and is wrapped in a green to blue-green [[bract|spathe]]. The yellowish or bluish-green [[spadix (botany)|spadix]] is up to 14 centimeters long. Fruiting is also rare, but the plant may produce red [[Berry (botany)|berries]] each 6 to 8 millimeters wide.<ref name=pier/><ref name=boyce/><ref name=china>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=3&taxon_id=200027137 ''Alocasia cucullata''.] Flora of China.</ref>

==Biology==
The flowers are [[pollination|pollinated]] by the [[drosophilidae|drosophilid flies]] ''[[Colocasiomyia alocasiae]]'' and ''[[Colocasiomyia xenalocasiae|C. xenalocasiae]]'', at least in [[Japan]].<ref name=mi>Miyake, T. and M. Yafuso. (2005). [http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1442-1984.2005.00139.x/abstract Pollination of ''Alocasia cucullata'' (Araceae) by two ''Colocasiomyia'' flies known to be specific pollinators for ''Alocasia odora''.] ''Plant Species Biology'' 20(3) 201–208.</ref>

The plant easily reproduces [[vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] sprouting up when pieces of stem or root enter the soil.<ref name=pier/>

It is susceptible to [[leaf spot|bacterial leaf spot disease]] caused by ''[[Pantoea agglomerans]]''.<ref name=rom>Romeiro, R. S., et al. (2006). [http://www.ndrs.org.uk/article.php?id=014051 Bacterial spot of Chinese taro (''Alocasia cucullata'') in Brazil induced by ''Pantoea agglomerans''.] ''New Disease Reports'' 14 51.</ref>

This species has been [[introduced species|introduced]] to many regions, including much of the Pacific, where it can be found in [[Hawaii]], [[Micronesia]], [[Fiji]], [[French Polynesia]], and [[Guam]]. It has also been introduced to parts of [[Central America]].<ref name=pier/>

==Human uses==
It has some uses in [[traditional Chinese medicine]]. It is applied externally to treat [[snakebite]], [[abscess]]es, [[rheumatism]], and [[arthritis]].<ref name=boyce/> It is poisonous due to the presence of [[calcium oxalate]] crystals.<ref name=ntbg/>

This plant is considered to bring good luck, so it is kept at [[Buddhist temple]]s in [[Laos]] and [[Thailand]].<ref name=china/>
